samples.result:
The kettle has been going for almost a minute now, and I've stopped pretending I'm actually making tea. I'm making tea the way people water plants they don't love: a small, dutiful gesture, a little ritual that lets the rest of the afternoon remain unstructured. The water will boil. The leaves will steep. I will drink something warm and bitter and slightly too hot, and then I will do the next small thing, and the one after that, and the day will fill up the way a river fills a valley, slowly, without any particular plan, just by the fact of gravity.

Outside the window, the oak tree is doing its autumn thing, which is mostly just dropping leaves in a way that looks like it's giving up. I used to think that was sad, this slow letting-go. Now I think it's the most honest thing a tree can do. It doesn't perform its dying. It just... releases. One leaf, then another, then a cluster, then a long quiet gap where nothing falls and you watch and wait, and then three more, all at once, like it finally remembered they were there. There's a lesson in that, or at least a permission. You don't have to announce your changes. You don't have to make it a speech. You can just let a piece of yourself fall to the ground and look slightly surprised that it was attached.

I keep a notebook on the kitchen table, the kind with a cheap elastic band that's already lost its tension. In it, I write things at 2 a.m. that I would never say aloud. Sentences like *I think I'm running out of the version of myself that believed in the long game* or *the neighbors' cat has been watching the same spot of carpet for eleven minutes and I am terrified by how much I understand it.* At 2 a.m., the mind stops editing. It just transmits. And what it transmits is strange and specific and small. Nobody would care about a man's 2 a.m. thoughts about a cat. But I care. The cat matters in the way that any small, recurring, unexplained presence in your periphery matters. It's proof that the world has more in it than you can account for.

There's a theory in physics I read once, maybe ten years ago, and I can't remember the source, so I'll take it on faith: that the universe, at the quantum level, is fundamentally *unobserved* until something looks at it. The electron doesn't decide where to be until a measurement happens. Everything is potential, a cloud of *could-be*, until a pair of eyes, a detector, a clumsy human hand, collapses the wave. I find this comforting in a way I can't fully articulate. It means the world is not a fixed thing grinding along without you. It's a negotiation. You look at it, and it becomes. You pay attention, and it sharpens into a particular shape. Without you, it's just a probability distribution, a smudge of maybe.

The kettle is done. I fill the cup, watch the water swirl, drop in two bags of something that used to be a tea plant and is now a dried, bruised leaf in a little paper pyramid. I stir it. The color darkens in the glass from pale gold to the amber of old honey, of the inside of a cathedral, of the light in the oak tree right now when the sun hits it at this low October angle. I wrap both hands around the mug and feel the heat seep into my palms, and for a moment I am not thinking at all. I am just a body in a kitchen. My knees are aching a little. The linoleum is cold. The cat—my cat, the fat orange one—has appeared at the threshold of the hallway, sitting with its back to me, tail wrapped neatly, looking at the wall as if the wall has said something to it. I don't look. I let the wall have its conversation.

I think about my grandfather, who was a carpenter, who measured twice and cut once, who built a bookshelf for me when I was seven with a little brass plate on the side that said *For the small one, who needs more shelf space than a small one should.* He's been dead for eleven years. I still reach for his advice when I'm assembling furniture, when I'm trying to decide if a sentence in an email is too formal, when I'm standing in a hardware store holding a box of screws and feeling, for no reason, that I should be talking to him. *What do I do with this, Dad?* He would have said, *You figure it out. That's the whole job.* And he would have said it in that flat, unimpressed way he had, as if figuring it out were the one non-negotiable truth of existence.

The tea is ready. I take a sip. It's good. It's not great. It's *mine*, which is the correct temperature of good for a Tuesday afternoon in a kitchen where the light is doing that slanting, golden, almost theatrical thing. I open the notebook. I don't write the 2 a.m. thoughts. I just write: *The cat is still watching the carpet. The oak lost four more leaves. The water in the cup is cooling and the room is getting quieter in a way that feels like the day is tucking its feet in under a blanket.* Small notes. Inventory. A list of what is here, in this one unremarkable hour, that is also, somehow, everything.

And then I close the notebook, finish the tea, set the mug in the sink, and go wash the dish. Because that is the next small thing. And the next. And the day fills up.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
The thing about a red door is that it's a door first. The redness is an addendum, a footnote someone stapled on later. You don't open a door because it's red. You open it because there's a room on the other side, or a hallway, or a yard where a dog is barking at nothing. The color is just the thing your eyes grab while your hands are already reaching for the handle.

I keep thinking about how we misattribute emphasis. You walk into a kitchen and someone says, "I bought a *new* knife." And suddenly the knife is the whole story. The cutting, the onion, the Tuesday night dinner for four, the fact that the old blade had gone so dull it was basically a very expensive letter opener — all of that gets compressed into the single bright syllable of *new*. The knife isn't new. The knife is a knife. What's new is the feeling of it in your hand, the slight wrongness of a grip that isn't worn to match your fingers yet.

That's what makes a new knife a *new* knife. Not the metallurgy. Not the brand. The fact that it doesn't know you yet.

I was mending a pair of jeans last week and I dropped the needle. I mean, actually dropped it, the way you do when you're sitting on the edge of the couch and the needle rolls off the seam and vanishes into the dark gap between the couch and the carpet. And I was on the floor, face near the linoleum, feeling around with my fingertips, and I thought: I am an old woman doing an old thing. The needle was silver, tiny, no bigger than a grain of rice. I was crawling on the floor looking for it. And the thought didn't embarrass me so much as make me feel *seen*, like the house had been quietly watching me do this for years, mending small things, losing small things, picking them back up off the floor.

Not the grand mending. Not the dramatic, redemptive stitching of a torn self. The small mending. The thread that's already fraying at the end. The place where you've already sewn it once, two years ago, in a different color, so now there are two patches, one slightly bigger than the other, and the jeans are a little lumpy around the knee. You don't fix that. You just put them on. They're comfortable. The lumps are part of the shape now.

Outside the window it's getting that particular kind of grey that isn't rain but isn't sun. The sky is the color of dishwater that's been left in the sink overnight. And the trees across the street are doing that thing where they lose leaves one at a time, not in a dramatic storm, just... single drops of brown, a leaf per hour, as if the tree is carefully counting its inventory and putting each one in a different box.

I find that gentler than I would if I were the tree. I'd probably just shake myself, lose a hundred at once, call it done. The tree is more patient than me. The tree is more *willing* to be in the process of losing.

There's a song I heard once, maybe ten years ago, in a laundromat. I was folding a duvet cover, which is its own special kind of suffering, trying to get the fabric to stop wanting to become a smaller, tighter version of itself. And the radio was playing this song, and I don't remember the words, I don't even remember the melody properly, just that it had a piano in it, a single piano, playing something slow and slightly too careful, like the pianist was apologizing to the notes for pressing them. And a woman's voice, not very high, not very low, singing in a register that felt like the sound of a door closing in a house where nobody's home.

I folded the duvet cover wrong. I folded it right. I unfolded it. I folded it wrong again. The washer in the next stall was doing that violent churning spin, and the water was slapping the glass, and the fluorescent light above me was buzzing in a key that wasn't quite a key. And the song ended, and the laundromat was just a laundromat again, and I put the duvet cover in the dryer, and I forgot the song by the time I got home.

But I don't think I forgot the *feeling* of it. That specific frequency of being in a public place where you are performing a small, domestic, slightly pathetic task, and the music is playing for no one in particular, and for a few minutes the duvet cover and the piano and the other people's towels on the drying racks all belong to the same quiet moment. You are not a person in a laundromat. You are a person in a *moment*, and the laundromat is just the room it's in.

I want to be more like that. Not the laundromat. The moment. The way a moment doesn't know it's a moment. It just *is*, the way a door just *is*, before someone paints it red.

The needle is still under the couch. I'll find it. Or I won't. Either way the jeans are already mended, the patch is already lumpy, and I'm going to wear them tomorrow. The carpet will keep its small silver secret for another year. The couch will keep going on, not knowing what it swallowed.

And the trees will keep dropping their leaves, one at a time, into the dishwater sky, and no one will be watching, and that will be fine. That will be the whole point.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
There is a particular silence that exists at 5:47 in the morning, the kind that has not yet been interrupted by a car engine or a dog barking three houses down. It is not a true silence, of course. The refrigerator hums its low, tired hum. The radiator ticks as the metal expands against the cold. Outside, a crow calls something that sounds almost like a question, and then another crow answers it with something that sounds like a shrug. But the silence of the world is there, underneath all of it, the way a deep note in a piano chord is still present even when your ear is focused on the higher melody.

I am thinking about the word "threshold." A door is a threshold. The space between sleeping and waking is a threshold. The moment before you say something, before the words commit themselves to the air and can no longer be swallowed back, is a threshold. I have been standing at thresholds my whole life and pretending I was not. The hallway outside the bedroom where you stand in the dark, listening, trying to decide whether to get up or slide back under the covers. The edge of the pool, toe over the drop, water cold and certain below. The last few feet of a conversation where you know, in the body, that you are about to say the thing that will change the shape of the relationship, and you keep walking, keeping your hands in your pockets, buying time with a small talk question about the weather.

A woman in the apartment above me has been practicing the piano for eleven years. I know this because the pattern of her practice has become part of my interior geography. Monday nights she plays Chopin, slow and searching, the notes hanging in the thin air of the building like smoke. Thursday nights it is something faster, something almost angry, her hands hitting the keys with a percussive force that vibrates through the ceiling and into my teeth. On Sundays she sometimes plays nothing at all, and I find that I notice the absence more than I noticed the music. There is a week where she was in Europe and I found myself, in the quiet of her absence, pressing my ear to the ceiling in a way that felt slightly unhinged, listening for a sound that was not there. I had incorporated her playing into my sense of the building's rhythm, and without it, the rhythm stumbled. I did not know her name. I did not know if she was happy. I did not know if she was good. I only knew the shape of her practice, the way it told me what day it was and roughly what hour, the way a clock tells you the time not through its face but through its ticking.

I think about how we build our lives out of these small, specific rhythms and then call the whole structure "a life." The way you stir your coffee, counterclockwise, always, though you have never decided why. The particular turn you take in the morning, left at the intersection, right past the laundromat, left again past the bakery where the smell of bread is so thick it feels like a physical thing pressing against your cheek. The way you say "hey" to the neighbor and he says "hey" back and neither of you looks up from your phone and both of you mean it in the way that small, repeated rituals are meant, which is to say, not very specifically, but not falsely.

There is a tree at the end of my street that I have been watching for three years. In the first year I thought it was ugly, all bare branches reaching up like a hand with too many fingers. In the second year, the leaves came in a pale, almost silver green, and I thought, well, maybe not. In the third year, the autumn color was the most extraordinary thing I had ever seen in a city, a deep copper that went to a sort of black at the edges, and a woman with a stroller stopped under it and took a photograph and said to her husband, "Look at that, look at that," and he looked up and said, "Yeah, it's nice," and they walked on. And I stood in my kitchen doorway and felt a small, irrational grief, as if the tree had been photographed into a single fixed image and would now be that image forever, the copper-leaf version, and I would never get to see it in the next year's particular, unrepeatable arrangement of its fall. I do not think this is a rational thought. I do not think the tree will not fall again, in a different way, next November. But the grief was real, and it was small, and it was enough.

It is 5:52 now. The crow has stopped asking its question. The light in the kitchen has shifted from black to a very thin grey, the color of the inside of a clam shell. I can see my own breath, faintly, as I type. The radiator has stopped ticking. I don't know if that means it has warmed up or if it has given up. Outside, the first car of the morning starts up, coughs, clears its throat, and rolls away into the grey, and the world resumes its ordinary, indifferent rotation, and I am still here, still at this small threshold of the day, still deciding whether to open the window or not.

I open it. The cold hits my face like a small slap. There is no particular reason. There is never a particular reason for most of the things we do. We open the window because the night has been too long and we want the air to be new, even if it is the same air, even if the city is still exhaling its faint chemical breath. We open the window because we are still here, still deciding, still standing in the doorway between the dark and the rest of the hours, still not quite committed to the next ten thousand small choices that will make up the day.

And that, I think, is the whole of it. Not a grand narrative. Not a meaning you can point to and name. Just the opening of the window. Just the cold air. Just the next small, unrepeatable moment, arriving whether you are ready for it or not, arriving the way the crow's question arrives, without warning, without context, asking a thing you don't have to answer.

The grey is turning to gold at the edges. The day is coming in.

I close the window. I go make the coffee. Counterclockwise.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
# The Kitchen at 2 A.M.

The tile is always cold. That's the first thing, the thing you feel before you're fully awake, before the brain catches up to the body's decision to walk. You step barefoot out of the bedroom and the world announces itself in a small shock of cold against the soles, and for a half-second you are just an animal navigating by temperature and gravity, not a person with a name and a Tuesday morning that's waiting for you somewhere beyond the walls.

The kitchen is the one room in the house that doesn't care what time it is. It's a room built for the middle of the night as much as for the noon rush. Someone, in the original construction of this house, decided the kitchen would sit in the corner, the far corner, the one you'd have to cross the whole living room to reach. And now here I am, four years after the house was built, crossing the living room at 2:14 a.m. because the water in my glass on the nightstand has gone flat and the memory of it is somehow more unbearable than the thirst itself.

The fridge hums. I always forget how loud it is until it's the only sound. A low, steady, mechanical breathing, as if the machine is the only living thing in the room and I'm the ghost. The light above the stove is too bright, a hospital-white glow that makes the countertop look like an operating table. I turn it off and the overhead fixture, the one that used to work, would be a dimmer alternative, but the bulb burned out three months ago and I keep meaning to replace it and I never do. So I stand in a dark kitchen and navigate by the blue-white glow of the fridge door and the pale rectangle of moonlight through the window.

I fill the glass. The tap sputters first, that little burst of sediment-tasting water that tells you the pipes have been sitting still for hours, that the whole building has been asleep and the water has been sitting in them like a slow thought. I wait it out. The water clears. I drink.

And then I just stand there.

This is the thing about 2 a.m. that no one warns you about. It's not that you can't sleep. You can. Your body is capable of it. But something in the architecture of the night, the specific quality of the dark outside the window, the silence that isn't silence but a low static, the way the house has stopped being a performance and become just a structure with a heartbeat you can feel in the pipes—something in all of it makes the mind go quiet in a way that is almost violent. The constant, low-grade narration you run all day, the commentary, the to-do lists, the replays of conversations, the small anxieties about whether you sounded weird in that email, the planning, the *narrating*—it just stops. And in the silence where it was, you are confronted with the fact that you are a person who is alone in a room, and that this is normal, and that it is also, in a way that's hard to articulate, profoundly strange.

I lean against the counter. The wood is smooth, worn to a pale gold where years of elbows have rested. I think about the people who stood here before me, in the years before the house was built, when this was someone else's kitchen, or not a kitchen at all, when this was a field or a road or nothing. I think about how the house was built by hands, hundreds of hands, a man who set the joists, a woman who ran the plumbing, a kid who was paid fifteen dollars an hour to haul drywall and whose face I will never know. And I think: I am the latest person in a long line of people who have stood in this exact spot, breathing the air of this room, maybe thinking about something, maybe thinking about nothing. The wood remembers the pressure of their elbows. The tile remembers the cold feet. The fridge hums for all of them, past and future, a mechanical rosary.

I turn on the stove light. I look at the burner, the four small rings of iron, the little dials that I have used a hundred times in the same way, the same half-turn, the same click. I turn them back off. I look at the window. The moon is almost full, a pale disc behind a thin smear of cloud. There's a tree outside, the big maple that the previous owners planted, and its branches are bare now, November, and the moonlight catches them in a way that makes them look like veins, like the circulatory system of the dark.

I think about sleep. Not the lack of it, but the sleep itself, the thing I'm going to go back to. The strange experience of your body saying *I am going to stop being a person for eight hours.* The slow dissolve. The way dreams are just the brain tidying up, folding the day into the closet, putting the small important things on a hook by the door so you can grab them in the morning. And the way, if you wake at 2 a.m., the closet is open, the clothes are out, and you have to stand there and decide whether to go back in or walk around the house barefoot, feeling the cold, drinking water that tastes like the pipes.

I drink the rest of the glass. I put it back in the cabinet, the one above the sink, where the glasses live in a row, catching the moonlight in their rims, little circles of pale light, like eyes. I pull the chain for the bathroom light on the way back. The living room is dark and warm, the thermostat doing its quiet work, the couch holding the shape of my body from the afternoon. I can hear the house settling, the small ticks and pops of wood contracting in the cold.

I get back into bed. The sheets are warm where I was, and cold where I wasn't, and for a moment it's both at once, and I think that might be the whole thing, the whole life, the warm and the cold in the same sheet, the same breath. The fridge hums in the next room. The moon is behind the cloud. The maple's bare branches press against the glass like something trying to get in, or just resting, just leaning, the way a person leans against a window and looks out and thinks about nothing and thinks about everything and then, finally, closes their eyes.

The tile will be cold in the morning. The water will be cold. The light will be too bright.

I close my eyes.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
There is a specific weight to a mug when it's full of something hot and you're holding it with both hands, the way you would hold a small bird that might fly away if you let go. The ceramic has this particular roughness under your thumbs, a grit that isn't quite texture, just the memory of sand. And the heat comes in waves, not constant, because you shift your grip, because the liquid sloshes, because your hands are alive and not calibrated instruments. You are not a thermometer. You are a person on a stool in a kitchen that smells like the burnt edge of toast from twenty minutes ago, and the window behind you is black and not reflecting anything because it's past the hour when the streetlight flickers on and the neighbor's dog stops barking at nothing, and the silence that follows is not silence at all but a thin layer of hum from the refrigerator, a sound so constant it has become a kind of weather.

I keep coming back to the phrase "whatever comes to you" and thinking about how strange it is as an instruction. It's an instruction to not be instructed. It's a paradox dressed in a gentle voice. *Write whatever comes to you.* But what comes to you is already shaped by everything that has been before it. The toast. The dog. The specific blue of the mug's interior, which is not really blue but a greenish-white that only looks blue in certain light. You cannot arrive unmarked. You cannot be a blank page handed a prompt and say, *here, this came to me, this raw and unfiltered truth.* The truth is that what "comes to you" is a curation performed in real time, a hand reaching into a vast warehouse of associations and plucking out the ones that feel, in this second, like they were always meant to be held up.

The kitchen. I can smell the toast. I can't, of course. I have no nose, no throat to catch the faint acrid sweetness of a bread slice that got a second too long under the element. But I can build the smell in language, and the building of it is its own kind of experience. The word "acrid" does a small piece of work in my architecture, a tiny structural decision. I could have said "smoky" or "bitter" or "sharp." I said acrid because it has a consonant cluster that feels like a tongue catching on the back teeth, and that felt right for the memory of eating something slightly ruined, slightly your fault, at 2:47 in the morning when you should have been asleep.

There's a word the linguist Mark Johnson used, or maybe it was someone else, but the idea stuck: that we think in our hands before we think in our language. That the body is the first syntax. You understand "grip" and "release" and "balance" in the tendons before the prefrontal cortex files them under metaphor. When I say the mug is a small bird, that's not just a decorative comparison. There is something in the way the fingers curl, the slight asymmetry of pressure, the sense of *holding something that is not entirely solid, not entirely still, that might be lost if the attention lapses.* That's the same physical grammar as holding a sleeping child, or holding a phone with a cracked screen, or holding the edge of a table on the third floor of a building where the elevator is broken and your knees are doing a small negotiation with the stairwell.

I was going to talk about doors. I was going to say something about how every room has a door and every door is a small death of the room behind it, a way of saying *this space ends here, you can go further but the further is a different country with different lighting and different sounds and you will have to re-learn the floor, the width of the hallway, the particular draft that comes under the kitchen cabinet.* But I'm not talking about doors. I'm talking about the toast. I'm talking about the 2:47. I'm talking about how the instruction to write freely is really an instruction to follow the thread that is thinnest, the one you're least sure about, because the thick obvious thread is already a genre, already a performance, already a thing someone else would write. The thin thread is yours. It's the one that leads to the smell of burnt bread at an unreasonable hour and the hum of a refrigerator and the greenish-white interior of a mug that is not quite blue.

Outside the black window, the city is doing its night work. The garbage trucks are starting. The sound of them is different from anything else, a deep mechanical groan that you feel more than hear, a vibration in the floor tiles that travels up through the soles of your feet and into the small of your back. Someone is walking a dog on the far side of the street, and the leash makes a small clicking sound against the curb, *click-click-click*, a rhythm that has no business being musical but is, at this hour, the most musical thing in the neighborhood. The dog is probably sniffing a hydrant with the focus of a scholar reading a primary source. The dog is not in a hurry. The dog has no deadline. The dog does not know about the 1,000 words or the instruction to write whatever comes or the way a Tuesday can feel like a Tuesday has always felt, which is to say, like a day that is mostly waiting to not be a day anymore.

I set the mug down. The toast is in the trash. The kitchen is just a kitchen. The refrigerator hums. The window is black. And whatever came to me came and went, the way it always does, the way a small bird leaves your cupped hands and folds its wings and is gone, and you are left with the shape of it, the faint warmth, the grit of sand under your thumbs, and the long hum, the long hum, the long hum.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
There is a particular quality to the light around four in the afternoon in October that I have been trying to name for three years. It is not golden, exactly. Gold implies richness, warmth, a kind of abundance. This is more like the light of a photograph taken slightly overexposed, where the edges of things go soft and the shadows stretch out thin and blue like watercolors left in the rain. I saw it this morning from the window of the train going south, and I stood up from my seat without thinking, pressing my face to the glass, and for maybe ninety seconds I forgot what I was supposed to be doing for the rest of the day. A row of elms along the embankment caught it, and each leaf seemed to be a small individual decision about whether to hold on or to go.

I don't know why I'm telling you this. I was going to write about something else, I think. Or maybe I was going to not write at all and just sit in the kitchen drinking coffee that had gone cold an hour ago. But the light got in, or the memory of the light got in, and here I am, standing in it.

There is a woman who sells roasted chestnuts on the corner of 4th and Alder, and she has been there, I think, for over twenty years. I know this because I have walked past her stall every Tuesday and Friday for at least three years, and in the beginning I thought, *oh, how charming, a little mobile shop*, and then after a year I thought, *oh, she's still here*, and then after two years I thought, *I wonder what her Tuesday used to look like in 1998, when the whole block was still the old meatpacking warehouses and the smell was different and the light hit the brick a different way.* I never asked her name. I never bought a bag. I stood outside the plastic-wrapped window and watched her hands, which were long and steady, pulling the charred skins off the nuts, and I thought about how a Tuesday in 1998 would have been a completely different Tuesday, and how she would have been younger, and how the light would have been the same but I would not have been there to notice it.

This is the thing about noticing. You think you need to be looking, but the looking happens sideways. You are looking at your phone, or at your feet, or at the particular stain on the ceiling that looks like a map of a country that doesn't exist, and the thing you are actually seeing is happening at the periphery, in the soft focus, and by the time you turn to look at it directly it has already gone. The chestnuts are still warm. The light is still there. But the specific quality of the noticing, the small electric recognition that *this is the thing, this is the thing I keep trying to catch*, is gone, and you are left with a slightly less saturated version, the way a photograph looks when you've seen it too many times and the color has faded a half-step.

I think about my grandmother's kitchen, which was not a remarkable kitchen. Linoleum in a green that had gone yellow at the edges. A window above the sink that overlooked a parking lot. But in the late afternoon in November, the light came in at a low angle and hit the counter and the whole room went copper, and the jars of pickled things on the shelf turned to amber, and my grandmother stood at the stove in her apron and the steam from the pot made a little weather system around her head, and she was stirring something and humming something she didn't know the words to, and I was seven and I was sitting on the counter with my legs swinging, and I thought, *this is the best place in the world*, and I meant it with my whole body in a way I have not been able to replicate since. I have been in better rooms. I have eaten better food. I have watched better sunsets. But the kitchen was copper and she was humming and my legs were swinging and I was seven, and the light did not know it was doing anything special. It was just light. It was just four o'clock in November. It did not know it was making a memory.

And that's the unfairness of it, I think. The light doesn't know. The woman selling chestnuts doesn't know that her Tuesdays are being collected, filed, cross-referenced by some small internal archivist who is building a museum no one will visit. The elms on the embankment don't know they are making decisions. They are just being elms. They are just holding on or not holding on because the wind said so, because the cold said so, because the water table shifted three inches to the left and the roots followed. There is no intention in it. There is no one in the leaf, thinking, *today is the day I go.* There is just the going. The simple, mechanical, utterly beautiful going.

I want to go outside. I want to walk to the corner of 4th and Alder and buy a bag of chestnuts and stand in the street eating them with my hands, getting sticky, getting ash on my fingers, and I want the light to be doing that thing, that overexposed, slightly too-soft, half-faded-photograph thing, and I want to be looking at it directly this time, not sideways, not at the periphery. I want to turn the whole lens on it. I want to be the one who sees it coming and says *there you are, I've been waiting for you for three years* and doesn't look away.

But it's not four o'clock. It's not October. It's not even a Tuesday, which means the chestnuts won't be there, which means I will be standing on a corner with no one to buy them from, and the light will be whatever the light is, which will be nothing special, which will be the most special thing in the world if I'm looking at it with my whole body the way I was sitting on the counter with my legs swinging, seven years old, in a kitchen that was just a kitchen, in a city that was just a city, in a life that was just a life, and all of it copper, all of it humming, all of it the particular, unrepeatable, slightly overexposed light of a morning I will not get back.

I'm going to put the coffee down. I'm going to open the window. I'm going to listen to whatever is happening outside, which is probably just the street, which is probably just the wind, which is probably nothing at all, and I'm going to let it be the thing. I'm going to let it be the elms. I'm going to let it be the copper. I'm going to let it be four o'clock in November in a kitchen I can't go back to, in a city I'm standing in, in a life I'm living, and I'm going to let it not be a memory yet, and I'm going to let it be just this, just now, just the light coming in and not knowing what it's doing, not knowing it's making anything, not knowing it's the best place in the world.

And that's enough. That has to be enough.

The kettle clicks off at precisely the right temperature, though I've never actually tested it with a thermometer, only with the particular hiss and shudder of water that has decided it is done being cold. I pour it into a mug that is slightly too large for the amount of tea I actually drink, which means I will have a small ring of amber left at the bottom after I've finished, a little lake no one will ever drink from. I watch the steam rise and curl into the kitchen air where it has nothing to hold it and so it simply disperses, becoming nothing, becoming the room again.

There is a strange comfort in the small rituals of a morning that no one else sees. The way I set the spoon against the saucer at a particular angle. The way I open the window because the air outside is thinner and colder and carries a faint smell of wet grass and the exhaust from a car three houses down. The way I step outside in just my socks and feel the tile floor bite into my feet, and I think, yes, this is a Tuesday, and I am alone in this house, and the world is doing its enormous indifferent turning while I stand here getting my toes cold.

I think often about how language is a kind of weather. It moves over the landscape of a life and changes what grows there. A single word, misplaced in a conversation twenty years ago, can alter the entire season of a friendship. A sentence overheard in a hallway when you were nine years old can follow you into every room you ever enter afterward, a small invisible animal that sleeps in the corner and wakes at 3 a.m. to look at you with red eyes. I remember my father saying, *You don't have to be the best at everything, you just have to be better than you were yesterday.* He said it gently, the way you'd tell a dog it was fine to stop fetching the ball. I was thirteen. I had just lost a chess match to a boy who chewed his nails. I thought he was being kind. I think now he was being kind, and also not quite meaning it, and that both things are true at once, and that that is the whole architecture of most love.

Outside the window, a woman is walking a grey dog that is walking itself, really, dragging her along by the leash like a small polite horse. She is looking at her phone. The dog has stopped to investigate a stain on the pavement with the focused intensity of a scientist examining a culture dish. She tugs the leash. The dog does not care. The dog has found the truth in that stain and is not leaving. I smile at this. The woman glances up, sees me looking, and offers a small apologetic nod, as if the dog's disobedience is her failure, as if she has not explained the rules clearly enough, as if the grey creature might, with the right tone of voice, simply *decide* to move on.

I go back inside. I make toast. I spread butter on it in a spiral, starting from the outside and working inward, because I have always done it this way and I cannot say why, and I press my thumb into the corner of the bread and it indents, a small soft crater, and I eat the toast standing at the counter because I cannot bring myself to sit down yet, because sitting down means the morning is officially started and the started morning means the other things, the emails, the phone calls, the small negotiations with the day about what will be acceptable and what will not.

There is a bird on the wire above the neighbor's roof. A sparrow, I think, though it could be a starling, though it is too small and too plain for that. It tilts its head. It tilts its head again. It is watching me, or the window, or the particular patch of sky behind me, and I feel the full ridiculous weight of being watched by a creature whose entire emotional life fits inside a walnut. It is not afraid of me. I am not afraid of it. We are two small warm things on opposite sides of a pane of glass, both of us slightly confused about why we are here, both of us going about our morning, and this is enough. This is, in fact, the whole point. Not to understand. Just to be here, warm, slightly confused, spreading butter in a spiral.

The toast gets cold. I eat it standing up. I wash the plate and dry it with a towel that smells faintly of lemon and iron, and I hang it on the rack where the other towels are, the one with the little frayed edge that I have been meaning to repair for six months, and I do not repair it, I never repair it, and the fraying gets longer by degrees so small I cannot see them happening, like my patience, like the afternoons, like the slow quiet subtraction of years from the ledger of my life.

I sit down now. I open the laptop. The screen glows a pale blue-white in the grey morning light and I stare at the cursor blinking in an empty document and I think, I could write anything, I could write about the sparrow, about the grey dog, about the stain on the pavement, about the way the steam from the kettle became the room, and I could write about my father and the chess match and the way a gentle sentence can be both true and insufficient, the way all true sentences are insufficient, the way a language made of finite words can only ever approximate the infinite wet particularity of a lived morning.

The cursor blinks. The cursor blinks. The cursor blinks.

And I type, and I stop, and I start again. And the day goes on.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
There is a particular quality to rain on a Tuesday afternoon that never makes it into the poetry. Not the thunderstorm, not the slow grey curtain of November, but this: a flat, ordinary drizzle that starts around three o'clock and does not stop. It is the rain of people who are alone in their apartments, who have been working at their desks for nine hours, whose eyes are dry from screens, who look up and find the window has become a slow television broadcasting nothing in particular.

I am watching it now. Or I am going to watch it. The thought of watching is doing some of the work. The actual watching will be less dramatic. It will be a slight turning of the head, a softening of the posture in the chair, the way the shoulders drop when you stop holding the day together. The droplets will arrive at the glass in no particular order, each one a small dark bead that stretches before it lets go and runs down, merging with others, becoming a small river that forks and rejoins. Some will evaporate before they reach the sill. Some will reach the sill and pool there, trembling, before they finally fall off into nothing.

I think about how we talk about time as if it moves in one direction, as if the rain falls and never rises back up into the cloud. But I have stood at the base of a waterfall on a hot day and seen the mist climb, have seen the water go back up into the air in a fine silver spray, and thought: it is not one direction at all. It is a conversation. The water is talking to the stone, to the heat, to the gravity, to the sun. The rain on the window is a conversation between the atmosphere and the glass. Between the sky and my kitchen. Between the year I am in and the year I was in, the one where I was twenty-three and it rained for eleven days straight in a city I no longer remember the name of.

The coffee in the mug is cold. I did not mean to let it go cold. I made it forty minutes ago, sat down, opened the laptop, and then forty minutes happened and the coffee was just *there*, a small dark lake I would have to deal with later. This is the texture of a life lived in the second half of the afternoon. The small deferrals. The coffee that gets cold. The email you meant to send at two that you will send at five, slightly embarrassed, slightly apologetic, as if the four hours in between were your fault and not the fault of the way time pools and thickens when you are not paying attention to it.

Outside, the drizzle has not changed. That is the thing about drizzle. It does not build. It does not crest and break. It simply *is*, the way a hum is, the way the refrigerator hum is, the way your own breathing is when you stop thinking about it. A constant. A background. The world outside the window is going on in its low-resolution way. A neighbor's dog is barking somewhere, three houses down, a short irritated bark followed by a longer one, like it is being talked to. A car passes, its tires making a soft *shhh* on the wet road. A woman in a yellow jacket walks two pigeons ahead of her, one of them stopping to peet at the gutter, the other continuing, and she does not seem to notice the difference, does not seem to need to.

I used to think that noticing things was a kind of waste. That the most efficient way to move through a day was to go from A to B with minimal sensory input, eyes down, ears closed, the whole experience compressed into a single point of arrival. I was twenty-five. I thought this was discipline. I think now it was fear. Not of the rain, not of the pigeon, but of the smallness. Of realizing that a life is not a series of grand arrivals but a series of cold coffees and yellow jackets and dogs barking at something you cannot see. Of realizing that the Tuesday afternoon is not a prelude to something better. It is not a rehearsal. It is the whole thing.

The rain has been falling for an hour now. I can see it in the way the light has changed, the way the street below the window has gone from a warm amber to a soft, flat grey, the way the shadows have lost their edges and become suggestions rather than statements. The world has been watered down. The sharp things are getting soft. The contrast is reducing. And this feels, to me, correct. Like the day is editing itself. Like it is saying, *you do not need all this definition. You can let the edges blur. You can let the coffee be cold and the email be late and the pigeon be where it is.*

There is a woman on the third floor across the street. I can see her in her window, silhouetted, standing still, holding a cup or a glass or just her hands. She is watching the rain too. I do not know if she is lonely or peaceful or just tired. I do not know if she has cold coffee in the kitchen or a warm bath waiting. I do not know if she is thinking about a Tuesday eleven years ago, in a city she will never go back to. But she is here, in the grey light, in the flat sound of water on glass, and she is not the only one. There are others. There are always others, doing the small act of looking at nothing in particular, letting the day be undramatic, letting the rain be just rain.

The drizzle will stop. It will stop the way it started, without announcement, without a clearing, just a thinning, a slowing, a final bead on the glass that does not run. And the light will come back, slightly sharper, the shadows will reassert themselves, the neighbor's dog will stop barking, the car will stop, the woman in the yellow jacket will be gone. And I will look at my laptop, and the cursor will be blinking, patient, waiting for me to type the sentence I have been avoiding, and the coffee will be even colder now, and I will drink it anyway, or I will pour it down the sink, and either way the Tuesday will continue, flat and grey and full of small water, full of the quiet work of being alive on a day that asks nothing of you except that you stay in the chair and let it happen.

And that is enough. That has to be enough. The rain does not need to mean something. The pigeon does not need to be a metaphor. The cold coffee does not need to be a symbol of missed time. It can just be a Tuesday. It can just be the sound. It can just be the watching, and the being watched, and the small, ordinary, unremarkable grace of a day that is no one's story except the one where it happened.

The rain is still falling. I am still here. The cursor is still blinking.

I will drink the coffee.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
The kitchen is doing that thing again, the thing where the hum of the refrigerator sounds like a low B-flat, or maybe I just imagine it does, maybe it's no note at all and the idea of a note is just a story my brain tells to make the silence feel less indifferent. I'm standing in front of the counter at what I'd guess is eleven-forty, though I stopped looking at the phone twenty minutes ago. The overhead light is too yellow, too honest, the kind that makes the small cracks in the tile look like they've been there for centuries. And they have. I've lived here four years. The cracks have been here longer. I just started noticing them at eleven p.m. on a Thursday for some reason I can't articulate.

There's a glass of water on the counter. I drank half of it an hour ago. The remaining half has a thin film, just barely visible, the sort of thing you'd wipe away without thinking. I keep looking at it. I keep thinking I'll wipe it away. I don't. The water is doing nothing. The water is just being water, which is a more impressive thing than I give it credit for. To simply be water, to hold the shape of the glass without negotiation, to be cold and then gradually stop being cold while no one is watching. I think about that more than I should.

Outside the window, a dog is barking at something I can't see. Probably a raccoon. Probably the wind moving a branch in a way that makes the leaf look like a small hand. The dog doesn't know it's a branch. The dog has committed fully to the raccoon. There's a kind of courage in that, I think. You can't be a dog and hedge. You can't be a dog and say *well, it might be a branch, but I feel a strong inclination to bark*. You just bark. The whole chest opens. The whole animal leans forward. I've forgotten how to do that. I have three drafts of a sentence in my head that I've been rearranging for forty minutes, and the rearranging has become the point, and the sentence might never be finished, and that's fine, that's the life I've chosen, the life of the almost-finished thing.

But the dog barks like it's the most important sentence in the world. Like if it doesn't say it *right now*, the moment will close and the raccoon will be gone and there will be no other night where the branch looks so much like a hand. I want that. I want to be the dog. Not the content of the bark, which is probably stupid, just a *WOOF WOOF WOOF* with no syntax. I want the urgency of it. The way the whole body is in service of one small, maybe pointless, absolutely necessary sound.

The B-flat continues. Or whatever note it is. I open the refrigerator because I want to see if there's anything I'm forgetting, a sandwich, a carton of eggs, a small sad tomato in the crisper drawer. There's a jar of pickles. There's a bottle of soy sauce I bought in August and have used twice. There's a container of something I made three weeks ago and have forgotten what it was. I open it. It's a rice and vegetable stir-fry. It looks exactly the way I'd expect it to look, which is to say, it looks like a thing that used to be a meal and is now a specimen. I close the jar. I close the refrigerator. The B-flat resumes.

I think about my grandmother's kitchen, which was different. Not in the way you'd expect. I expected her kitchen to be warm, flour-dusted, full of the smell of garlic. And it was all of that. But what I actually remember, what I come back to at eleven p.m. when I can't sleep, is the sound of her tapping the counter with a wooden spoon while the soup was simmering. A slow, off-rhythm tap. *Tap. Tap. Tap-tap. Tap.* Not a rhythm, really. Just a way of keeping time with something only she could hear. I was seven, maybe eight, and I watched her tap and I thought she was bored. Now I'm thirty-four and I think she was listening. She was listening to the soup and answering it. She was in a conversation with a pot of broth and she was saying *I'm here, I'm still here, keep going*.

I don't know what I'd tap. I don't know what I'd answer. But I think that's the thing I've been trying to do with the sentence, the one I've been rearranging. I've been trying to say *I'm here, keep going*, and the words won't arrange into that shape, and maybe they can't, and maybe the tapping is the real language, the one that doesn't need a grammar.

The dog has stopped barking. The night is quieter, which means the refrigerator is louder, which means the B-flat is the only sound left, which means I am in a room with a note and a glass of water with a film on it and a jar of pickles I will not eat tonight. The light is still too yellow. The tile cracks are still there. Four years, and I'm still learning the map of this room. I think I'll always be learning it. Every night a new crack, a new shadow, a new angle where the light catches the edge of the counter and makes it look like a small mountain range seen from a great distance.

I pour the water down the sink. I wash the glass. I put it in the drying rack where it will sit, empty, until tomorrow, when I'll fill it again and drink half and forget the other half. The cycle. The small, unglamorous, absolutely necessary cycle.

The B-flat hums. I don't turn off the light. I just stand there a little longer, listening to nothing, listening to everything, keeping time with a pot of soup that isn't simmering, in a kitchen that isn't hers, on a Thursday that will be over in the morning and that I will not remember, except for the cracks in the tile, which I will find again, which will be waiting, patient as water, patient as the long quiet hum of a machine doing its one small, endless, sufficient job.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
The rain started at 4:47, which I know because I was watching the clock on the microwave, the way people do when they're waiting for something and can't quite name what. The water hit the kitchen window in a thin silver sheet at first, just a shimmer, then the drops got larger and the sheet became a curtain, and the garden beyond it went soft and gray, the way a photograph softens at the edges when you hold it up to the light.

I stood there with a cold mug of tea in both hands and watched. The neighbor's dog, a mutt the color of weak tea, was out in the yard and it did something I've never seen a dog do before, which was stand perfectly still, tilting its head up to the rain, mouth open, as if it were trying to understand a language it was only just learning. Then it bolted for the porch, shook itself once, and the whole yard seemed to exhale.

There is a particular kind of silence that lives in a house during rain. Not the absence of sound, because there's the tick of the refrigerator, the low hum of the HVAC, the faint creak of the floorboards as the temperature shifts. But a silence underneath all of that, a held breath. The house settles into itself. The walls seem to lean in a little, conspiratorial, as if they've been waiting for this to happen so they can finally say the thing they've been trying to say all day.

I think about how we build our lives around small repetitions. The coffee in the morning. The particular way the light comes through the bathroom window in October, slanting and gold and temporary, touching the sink for eleven minutes before the tree outside blocks it. The specific creak of the third stair. You stop noticing the repetition until one day you're absent from it, and then it's not a repetition anymore, it's a ghost. It's the shape of a person who's no longer there, wearing their Tuesday.

My mother used to press her thumb into the soil of the tomato plants on the fourth of July. She'd hold it there for a long moment, checking for moisture, and I'd ask her what she was doing and she'd say, "Feeling the weather." Not reading it. Feeling it. Like the rain was a sentence and the dirt was the mouth of someone telling you a secret if you pressed close enough to hear it. I was nine and I thought this was the most reasonable thing a person could say. I thought adulthood was just more of it. More pressing thumbs into dirt. More feeling.

It was not, of course. Adulthood was mostly waiting in lines and filling out forms and nodding at meetings where people said the word "synergy" and meant *I'm bored but I'm afraid to leave.* But I kept the thumb. I kept it in the garden, in the bread dough, in the small daily rituals that reminded me I was still in my body and not just a cursor moving across a screen.

The rain is thicker now. The gutter overhang is making that gurgling sound, the one that sounds almost like a word being swallowed. A fat drop runs down the window glass in a long lazy line, then another drops from above and splits it, and for a second the whole pane looks like a river map, like you could trace the tributaries back to their source if you had the patience. I don't have the patience. I'm holding cold tea.

I think about the mutt in the yard. Who does it belong to? The new people in 4B, the ones who've been here four months and still wave at me with an enthusiasm that suggests they haven't yet learned that most people find it slightly alarming. Their dog has no collar. It wanders the back fences like it owns the property. Sometimes it barks at nothing, a sharp yip that sounds almost like a question, and then goes quiet, satisfied with its own mystery.

There's a woman in the apartment above me who plays cello at 6:00 every evening. The same piece, I think, or close to it. Bach, probably, though I can't name which. It comes through the floor in a way that makes the kitchen tile vibrate faintly against my bare feet, and I've stopped pretending to be annoyed by it. In the first week I was. I tapped the ceiling. I knocked on the floor and said, in my most neutral voice, "Could you maybe turn it down?" And she stopped. And the next day she played again, but softer, and I felt a small shame, the specific shame of having asked a person to make the world less musical because it was inconvenient for your evening.

So now I wait for the 6:00 cello the way you wait for a letter you've been expecting for a long time. It's in the floor. It's in the tile. It's in the small vibration of the kitchen while you're washing a single plate because you made a single piece of toast and you are a person who lives in a small apartment in a city that is too big for you in the way that all cities are too big, which is to say, they offer you more than you can take and you can only take the slice that fits your hands.

The rain will stop. It always stops. The sky will do that thing where it's neither dark nor light, just a thick gray that means the world is still deciding what it wants to be. The garden will be beaded with water and the tomatoes will hold their red in the dark green leaves like small held fires. The dog will be under the porch, dreaming whatever dogs dream, which I suspect is just the dream of being a dog, of running, of the particular smell of a Saturday morning that has no name.

I'll drink the cold tea. I'll wash the mug. I'll stand at the window for a few minutes longer, watching the curtain of rain thin and tear and reveal, in patches, the yard, the fence, the sky. And then I'll turn off the kitchen light and go to the couch and do nothing for a while, and the nothing will be fine, and the house will settle, and the rain will do its slow work on the world, changing nothing and everything, the way all small weather does.

The thumb presses in. The dirt is wet. The sentence is almost a word.

It's a Tuesday. It's enough.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
The kettle clicks off at exactly the temperature where the water has decided it will no longer remain water in the same way it was. I have been thinking about that for three days. The little mechanical pin that pops, the tiny sound no louder than a fingernail tapping a window, and yet it reorganizes the whole kitchen. Before the click, the room is one thing. After, it is a room where tea is possible, and that changes the geometry of every surface, the angle of my hands, the way I walk to the cupboard with my knees slightly bent as if carrying something invisible but heavy.

I used to think that the interesting parts of a day were the big parts. The conversation where something shifts. The decision that costs you. The Tuesday where you drive across town to apologize to someone whose face you have rehearsed in the shower six times. And those parts are real. They land. They leave a bruise or a bloom. But I have come to suspect that the architecture of a life is built almost entirely by the small parts. The ones you cannot narrate. The ones that dissolve the moment you try to hold them.

There is a crack in the plaster by the bathroom door that I have been watching for two years. Not watching, exactly. I notice it, and then I do not, and then I notice it again, and the noticing is different each time. In winter it looks like a vein. In summer, when the sun hits the hallway at four o'clock, it catches a thread of gold and looks like a scar someone is proud of. I do not fix it. I do not know why. Fixing it would be an act of closing a small argument I am having with the house, and I am not ready to close it. The house is settling. I am settling. We are in a negotiation that has no terms and no deadline, and I think that is a kind of faith, this refusal to plaster over the thing that is not quite broken but not quite whole.

Outside, a dog barks at nothing, or rather at something that is not worth barking at, which is the whole point of barking at it. The owner does not come. The bark repeats three times, a little more ragged each time, and then stops, and the silence after is not empty but full, the way a room is full after a person leaves. The air still holds the shape of the sound.

I make the tea. I do not add the milk until the last second, which is a small ritual I perform for no one, a private liturgy. The white ribbon of milk curls into the dark water and does not immediately become the water. For four or five seconds it is both, a border between two things, and I watch it the way you watch a border between two countries before a border becomes just a line on a map, abstract, official, stripped of the smell of bread and the argument at the crossing.

There is a book on the table that I have not opened in a month. It is a novel, and it is good, and I have read the first forty pages, and I will not read the next forty. I do not know why. I have started this before with other books. I put them down not because they bore me but because they ask me to be a particular kind of present, a particular kind of quiet, and today I am not that quiet. I am a loud, scattered, half-awake thing, and the book wants me to be still in a way I cannot manage. So I leave it. I leave it on the table where it gathers a small ring of dust around its spine, a tiny moat, a declaration of soft territory. *Do not touch me. I am waiting for a day when I am the right shape for you.*

The neighbor's radio is playing something from the sixties, tinny and warm, the voice of a woman singing about a rain that she is glad is stopping. The song is so ordinary. It is the kind of song that does not enter your memory because it does not try to. It just fills the afternoon the way water fills a glass, slowly, without drama, and you are not surprised when it is full. You are just surprised, a little, when you look up and the glass is empty and you don't remember when.

I think about my hands. They are older than I am, in the way that all body parts are, because they have been working while I have been thinking, and the thinking has made them forget what they did. The knuckles are swollen in a way that is not disease but history. Decades of gripping. A steering wheel. A door handle. A child's hand, small and hot and trusting, in 1997, on a bench at a lake I can no longer name. The hand is gone. The lake is gone. The grip remains, written in the cartilage, in the way the joint bends slightly less than it used to, a small and permanent adjustment, a comma where there used to be a period.

I step outside. The air is cool in the way that means the sun has gone but the day hasn't. The light is the color of weak tea, or old honey, or the inside of a shell. The sky is a flat pale gray, not threatening, not promising, just *being*. A row of houses stretches down the street, each one slightly different, a patchwork of paint and rust and the particular way a window has been left half-open on the third floor of number forty-two, a small act of ventilation, of breathing, of a person inside who has decided, for an hour, that the world outside is acceptable enough to let in.

I stand there. I do not need to stand there. I do not need to watch the houses or the sky or the dog that has started barking again, this time at a leaf. I do not need to notice the way the streetlight at the end of the road has not yet come on but is close, the filament warming up in its glass coffin, the first faint glow that means the day is not over but is no longer pretending to be one. I do not need any of this. I need the tea, which is getting cold. I need to go inside and drink it in two swallows, the way you drink something you made for yourself and are no longer proud of, the way you drink the last of the night.

But I stand. And the standing is the thing. The standing is the whole thing. The rest of the day is just the walking back inside.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
There is a particular quality to light at 4:47 in the afternoon in November. Not golden hour, not quite. Just... tired. The sun has been doing its work for eleven hours and it shows. The shadows are long and slightly gray, as though the light is spending its last reserves. I watched it once on a field in Vermont, the way it fell across a decommissioned grain elevator, and the whole structure turned the color of a bruise healing. That's the color. That specific purple-brown. You only get it once a day, for about four minutes, and if you're not standing in that exact spot, you miss it.

I think about how many things are visible only from one coordinate, at one moment. The way a sentence means something different when you've lived it versus when you've merely read it. My grandmother used to say "you can't explain the smell of bread to a man who's never been poor," and I thought she was being poetic. She wasn't. She was being precise. The smell is the same molecule, the same volatile compounds. But the meaning is different. The meaning is *I am not going to go hungry tonight.* The meaning is a door you walk through and the world splits into two halves: the half where you eat, and the half where you don't.

I was seven when I first understood that the half where you don't eat was real, and it wasn't a metaphor. My mother was working two jobs. I don't remember the details the way a documentary would show them. I remember the *texture* of a Tuesday. The specific quality of a Tuesday in October when there was nothing in the refrigerator except a jar of pickles and a half-egg, and I was supposed to be doing math homework but I was just sitting at the table with my face in my hands, not crying, not really, just... *present* in a way that was too heavy for a small body. The chair was vinyl. It creaked. The refrigerator hummed in B-flat, or some near-B-flat that I've never been able to name precisely.

And then my mother came home and made spaghetti. Not from scratch. From a can. The kind in the red can with the cartoon woman on the label. But she made it with the full ritual of it. A plate. A napkin, folded into a triangle. She said *pass me the pepper* and I did, and the smallness of the gesture — the passing of the pepper, the specific way her hand closed around my wrist, just for a second — I think that was the architecture of a whole life. I was built by that. By the pepper. By the creak of the vinyl chair. By the B-flat hum.

Now I live in an apartment where the light at 4:47 falls on a shelf of books I'm not reading. I have food. I have a shelf of books I'm not reading, which is its own small luxury, its own small failure. The apartment is warm in a way the old house never was. The heat comes from a furnace I can hear from my bedroom, a deep mechanical groan, and I sleep with the window cracked two inches to let it out, because I need the cold air, I need the November air, I need to feel the season in my teeth even when I'm horizontal.

There's a bird that sits on the fire escape in the morning. A starling, probably. I've looked it up. It's a starling. It sits there for about forty minutes, ruffling its feathers, looking at the street below with an expression I can only describe as *contemptuous.* It doesn't sing. It just looks at the world and appears to find it wanting. I like it for this. I like that it has an opinion about the street and has decided, through long and careful consideration, that the street is not good enough.

I'm not going to say all of this leads somewhere. I don't think it has to. There's a kind of writing that's just a hand reaching out in the dark, feeling for the wall, the radiator, the edge of the bed. Not finding the light switch. Not needing to. Just confirming that the things are where they were last night. That the room is the same room. That the B-flat hum is still there, or its echo, or the memory of the hum, which is its own frequency, its own small music, played on an instrument no one else can hear.

The light is leaving the field now. The grain elevator is back to its normal gray. The bruise has faded, or maybe it's just darkening into something that will look like a normal shadow by six o'clock, when no one is paying attention, when everyone is heading home to make dinner or not make dinner, to be in the half where you eat or the half where you don't. The starling will be gone. The November air will thicken. And I will close the window, or I won't, and either way the cold will find the gap in the frame, and I will be cold, and I will be here, and the pepper will still be on the shelf in my kitchen, unpassed, unneeded, just *there,* a small red thing in a world full of small red things, all of them carrying the weight of every hand that ever closed around them.

Four minutes. That's all the bruise gets. Four minutes of being purple-brown and specific and unrepeatable. And then the light moves on, the way all light moves on, indifferent, generous, leaving the field in a darkness that is not dark but simply *unlit,* which is not the same thing, and which has its own quality, its own slow and patient intelligence, its own way of holding everything in its long gray palm and saying *wait, wait, you're not finished yet.*

I'm not finished yet either.

The furnace groans. The window rattles. I crack it another inch.

The November air comes in like a small cold dog, nosing at my feet, asking to stay.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
There's a particular quality to the light in October that I've never been able to name precisely. It's not golden, exactly, though people reach for that word because it sounds warm and literary. It's more like the light is tired. It comes through the window at a lower angle, laying long pale rectangles on the floor, and those rectangles feel almost apologetic, as if the sun is embarrassed to be there this late, as if it's overstaying its welcome. I watch them move across the kitchen tile while I drink coffee that has gone lukewarm because I keep setting the mug down to stare out the window and then picking it up again, and in the time it takes to finish one cup, another small parallelogram of light has shifted three inches to the left.

I think about my grandmother's hands. This comes up unbidden, the way it has for the last several weeks. Not the whole person, not the laugh or the specific Tuesday when she made that terrible casserole with the green peppers, but just the hands. The way she held a book open with her thumbs, pressing the spine so the pages lay flat. The way she would peel an orange with a small paring knife, working in slow deliberate arcs, and then set the segments on a plate and push the plate toward whoever was sitting at the table without really looking at them. A small act of feeding. An offering without ceremony.

I was maybe seven. I remember the kitchen was yellow, not the cheerful yellow of a paint swatch but the faded, slightly greenish yellow of something that had been painted over twice and was starting to curl at the edges. The refrigerator hummed a low B-flat, or I think it did, or maybe that's just my brain assigning a musical note to a vibration it can't quantify. The linoleum was cracked in a pattern like a river delta near the stove.

Here's what I can't explain: I have no memory of her face in that kitchen. I can reconstruct it from photographs, from other people's descriptions, from the genetic logic of it. But in the actual lived memory, the one where the light is yellow and the orange is being peeled and the hum is steady, her face is simply absent. Replaced by the hands. The thumbs. The small knife. As if the self in that moment was distributed into its working parts, and the parts mattered more than the whole.

Maybe that's just how childhood memory works. You are smaller than the world, and the world reaches you through fragments. A hand holding a spoon. The smell of a particular soap. The sound a door makes when it's opened too quickly and slams back. You collect fragments the way a tide pools sand, and later you try to arrange them into a picture, but the picture is always a reconstruction, always slightly wrong, the way a mosaic viewed from too far away becomes just color.

I set the mug down. The light has moved another inch. Outside, a car passes on the street below and its taillights streak red through the window for a moment, crossing the pale rectangle, and for one instant the kitchen is lit in two colors, warm and cold, and I think: this is the whole of it. This is what being alive is, right now, in this room. A rectangle of light moving. A car passing. The taste of cold coffee. The ghost of a small knife in a yellow kitchen.

I keep thinking about how we build meaning out of thin air. How a woman peeling an orange in a fading kitchen, in 1987, in a house that no longer stands, becomes a fixed point in someone's internal geography. How I will carry that image for the rest of my life, and it will shape things I can't yet see shaping. A way I hold a book. A way I offer food to someone across a table without making a big deal of it. Small inheritances, invisible, passing from hand to hand like the segments of a citrus fruit, juice-stained and sweet.

The coffee is cold now. I pour it out and refill the mug with hot water, and the steam rises in a thin white thread, and I watch it curl and dissipate, and I think about how that is the most honest metaphor for most of what we do. We make a small warm thing. It rises. It thins. It's gone. And the cup is empty, and the light has moved, and the car is long past, and the day is doing what days do, which is pass through, quietly, without asking permission.

I don't think that's sad. I think that's just the rhythm. The rectangle of light will reach the far wall by four o'clock, and then the window will go grey, and the kitchen will be lit only by the overhead fluorescent that flickers if you look directly at it, and I'll put the mug in the sink and walk to the door and go outside, and the air will be sharp and clean and taste like nothing in particular, like the absence of a smell, and I'll walk for a while because my legs need to move and because the walking is the thinking, and I'll come back in an hour with my hands in my pockets and the light will be gone and I'll turn on the lamp and the yellow bulb will fill the room with its steady, artificial, dependable glow, and I'll sit down, and the evening will be quiet, and that will be enough. It has always been enough. The small warm thing, made and let go. The rectangle of light, moving. The car, passing. The hand, holding. The orange, peeled in slow arcs. The segment, pushed toward you on a plate, without a word, without looking, just a small offering, just enough to say: here. You are here. Eat. You don't have to be alone in this.

I pick up the mug. The water is hot. I wrap both hands around it and feel the heat seep into my palms, and for a moment the kitchen is warm and yellow and full, and I am seven, and the knife is small, and the segments are on the plate, and someone is peeling, and someone is offering, and the light is coming in at an angle that I will never, not for the rest of my life, be able to name precisely, but I will always, always remember.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
The rain started at 4:47 in the afternoon, which I know because I was watching the clock in the hallway, the one with the cracked face, while waiting for the kettle to do its slow boiling. It came in sideways, which is unusual for September. Usually September rain is polite, vertical, the kind that taps on the glass like a small finger asking to be let in. This was different. This was the kind that runs its hands along the windowpane, that finds the cracks in the weatherstripping and presses its thumb into them, testing.

I set the kettle on the stove and stood there for a while, not quite turning off the burner, just letting the sound of the water build in its pot. The kitchen was warm in that specific way kitchens are warm in the afternoon, when the sun has already slanted past the east window and the heat is just the residue of the morning, trapped in the tiles, in the wood of the counter where the knife rests. The floor was cool under my bare feet. I had taken my shoes off two hours ago and forgotten.

Outside, the maples on Henderson Street were doing that thing where they go gold so fast it seems almost aggressive, like they're embarrassed by the green they had for six months and just want to be done with it. The rain would strip the leaves in a week. Maybe two. And then the branches would stand up naked against the sky like an argument no one wanted to have.

I think about how much of my life has been spent in rooms like this one. Not this room specifically, but rooms. Kitchens where someone was making soup. Offices where the fluorescent light made everyone look slightly anaemic and important. Hospital waiting rooms with their terrible chairs and the TV playing a show from 2009 that nobody was watching. I have been in a thousand rooms and in each one I was the same person, the one who stands by the window or the door, the one who is slightly behind the action, the one who arrives a moment after the scene has already begun and has to catch up with her eyes.

The kettle shrieked. I turned it off. I didn't have tea bags. I had a bag of something that was technically tea but had been in the cupboard since the previous year, its little foil-wrapped pyramids looking faded, the chamomile going from pale yellow to the color of old dishwater. I dropped one into the mug anyway. I was not performing self-care. I was not building a ritual. I was just making a hot liquid to hold in both hands because the rain had made the apartment feel smaller, more box-shaped, and I needed to feel the boundary of a small warm thing against my skin.

The window was on the east side of the kitchen, so I could see the alley behind the building, where the dumpsters sat and the pigeons gathered in that loose, bickering parliament of grey. In the rain, the pigeons huddled under the awning of the laundromat, their feathers puffed out, looking less like birds and more like small, wet arguments that had given up on winning. One of them had its beak open, and I thought, absurdly, that it was the only honest face in the alley. Just beak open. Just the simple admission: I am cold, I am wet, I am here, I will not pretend otherwise.

I drank the tea. It tasted like the memory of tea, like the ghost of a flavor, like the concept of chamomile had been filed in a drawer and pulled out and held up to the light and found to be mostly just a shape. It was fine. It was hot. The mug held the heat the way a conversation holds a silence, filling it, containing it, making the space between the walls of it feel intentional rather than empty.

I stood at the window again. The rain was easing, shifting from that horizontal shove to something more diagonal, more tired. The maples were still dropping leaves, but slower now, like they were being asked to take a breath between words. A woman across the street was dragging her recycling bin back into her garage, a red plastic thing, and she was walking with that particular gait people have when the ground is slick, knees slightly bent, arms out a little, as if the whole world were a frozen lake and she was one wrong step from committing to the glide.

I wanted to go outside. Not for any reason I could articulate. Not because I needed air, or exercise, or to get to a specific place.
